blocks.text: General introduction to carbonyl compounds

Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are the three most important families of **carbonyl compounds**, compounds that contain the carbonyl group, $\mathrm{C{=}O}$. They sit at the centre of organic chemistry: they are made from alcohols and alkenes, and they are the starting points for esters, amides, polymers, dyes, perfumes and drugs.

The three families differ in what is attached to the carbonyl carbon:

- In an **aldehyde**, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen: $\mathrm{R{-}CHO}$ (with $\mathrm{R = H}$ in methanal).
- In a **ketone**, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups: $\mathrm{R{-}CO{-}R'}$.
- In a **carboxylic acid**, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group: $\mathrm{R{-}COOH}$.

An organic compound in which the carbonyl group is attached to a hydrogen atom and to a carbon group (or to a second hydrogen in methanal). General formula $\mathrm{R{-}CHO}$; the functional group $-\mathrm{CHO}$ is always at the end of a carbon chain.
An organic compound in which the carbonyl group is bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups, $\mathrm{R{-}CO{-}R'}$. The carbonyl carbon is inside the chain.
An organic compound containing the carboxyl group, $-\mathrm{COOH}$, formed by joining a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group on the same carbon. General formula $\mathrm{R{-}COOH}$.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones undergo **nucleophilic addition** at the carbonyl carbon. Carboxylic acids are different: the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group changes their behaviour, and their typical reactions are acid-base reactions and *nucleophilic substitution* at the carboxyl carbon.
Nomenclature of aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids

**Common names** use the older names of the parent acids. Aldehydes and acids share the same stems: formaldehyde and formic acid (one carbon), acetaldehyde and acetic acid (two carbons), propionaldehyde and propionic acid, butyraldehyde and butyric acid. Positions of substituents are marked by Greek letters, $\alpha$ for the carbon next to the functional group, then $\beta$, $\gamma$ and so on. Ketones are named by listing the groups on the carbonyl carbon in alphabetical order followed by the word ketone (ethyl methyl ketone) with the exception of acetone, benzophenone and acetophenone.

**IUPAC names.**

- **Aldehydes:** replace the final $-e$ of the alkane by $-al$. The $-\mathrm{CHO}$ carbon is always carbon 1, so no number is needed for it. $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}$ is propanal; $\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)CHO}$ is 2-methylpropanal.
- **Ketones:** replace $-e$ by $-one$ and number the chain from the end that gives the carbonyl carbon the lowest number. $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ is propanone; $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}$ is butan-2-one; $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3}$ is pentan-3-one.
- **Carboxylic acids:** replace $-e$ by $-oic\ acid$. The $-\mathrm{COOH}$ carbon is carbon 1. $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$ is propanoic acid; $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)COOH}$ is 2-chloropropanoic acid.
- **Aromatic compounds:** $\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}$ is benzaldehyde (benzenecarbaldehyde), $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$ is acetophenone (1-phenylethanone), $\mathrm{C_6H_5COC_6H_5}$ is benzophenone (diphenylmethanone), and $\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$ is benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid).

blocks.problem: Write the IUPAC names of (a) $\mathrm{CH_3CH(CH_3)CH_2CHO}$, (b) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COCH_2CH_3}$, (c) $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2COOH}$ and (d) $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}$.
blocks.solution:
(a) The chain containing the aldehyde carbon is four carbons long (butane). The -CHO carbon is C-1, and the methyl group is on C-3, so the name is 3-methylbutanal.

(b) Five carbons with the carbonyl carbon in the middle: numbering from either end gives 3, so the name is pentan-3-one.

(c) The acid carbon is C-1. The chain has four carbons (butane) and bromine is on C-3, so the name is 3-bromobutanoic acid.

(d) The chain has four carbons with the -CHO as C-1 and a double bond between C-2 and C-3. The name is but-2-enal.

blocks.text: **Common mistake.** Do not give a position number to the aldehyde group: in propanal the $-\mathrm{CHO}$ is automatically on carbon 1. For a ketone the position is needed from butanone onward (butan-2-one) because the carbonyl can sit at different places.
Structure of the carbonyl group

The carbonyl carbon is **$sp^2$ hybridised**. It forms three sigma bonds in one plane (to oxygen and to two other atoms), with bond angles of about $120^\circ$. The remaining unhybridised $p$ orbital on carbon overlaps sideways with a $p$ orbital on oxygen to make the $\pi$ bond, which lies above and below the plane. The oxygen atom also has two lone pairs in $sp^2$ orbitals in the plane. So the $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ group is **planar and trigonal** around carbon.

Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so the $\pi$ electrons are pulled towards oxygen. The carbonyl group is strongly polarised, with a partial positive charge on carbon and a partial negative charge on oxygen. This polarity can be shown with two resonance forms, in one of which the carbon bears a full positive charge and the oxygen a full negative charge.
Polarisation of the carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon is an electrophile (attacked by nucleophiles) and the oxygen is nucleophilic and basic (it can be protonated).

Because of this polarity, aldehydes and ketones have higher dipole moments and higher boiling points than non-polar compounds of similar mass. It also explains the characteristic reaction: **nucleophilic addition**. A nucleophile attacks the planar, positive carbonyl carbon from either face, the $\pi$ bond breaks and the electrons move to oxygen, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that then takes up a proton.

**Why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones.** There are two reasons. *Electronic:* the two alkyl groups of a ketone push electrons towards the carbonyl carbon (the $+I$ effect) and reduce its positive charge, while an aldehyde has only one such group. *Steric:* two bulky groups of a ketone hinder the approach of the nucleophile and crowd the tetrahedral product. The order of reactivity is therefore $\mathrm{HCHO > RCHO > RCOR'}$. **Aromatic aldehydes** such as benzaldehyde are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes, because the carbonyl group is conjugated with the ring and the resonance reduces the positive charge on carbon.
Carbonyl carbon: $sp^2$, trigonal planar, $120^\circ$, electrophilic. Order of reactivity towards nucleophiles: methanal > other aliphatic aldehydes > aromatic aldehydes > ketones.
Methods of preparation of aldehydes and ketones

**Preparation of aldehydes.**

*By oxidation of primary alcohols* with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate), or by passing the alcohol vapour over copper at 573 K (dehydrogenation).

*By ozonolysis of alkenes.* Treating an alkene with ozone and then reducing with zinc and water splits the double bond and gives aldehydes (or ketones, depending on the substituents).

*By Rosenmund reduction.* An acyl chloride is hydrogenated over palladium on barium sulphate. The catalyst is partially poisoned to stop the reduction at the aldehyde and prevent over-reduction to the alcohol.
Rosenmund reduction.

*By Stephen reaction.* A nitrile is reduced by stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid to an imine salt, which is hydrolysed to the aldehyde. A nitrile or an ester can also be partially reduced to an aldehyde with DIBAL-H followed by water.
Stephen reaction.

*Aromatic aldehydes.* **Etard reaction:** toluene is oxidised by chromyl chloride ($\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}$) in carbon disulphide to a chromium complex, which is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde. Alternatively, side-chain chlorination of toluene gives benzal chloride, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde. **Gattermann-Koch reaction:** benzene reacts with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and a little cuprous chloride, and benzaldehyde is formed.
Etard reaction.
Gattermann-Koch reaction.

**Preparation of ketones.**

*By oxidation of secondary alcohols* with common oxidising agents such as chromic acid, or by dehydrogenation over copper at 573 K.

*By hydration of alkynes.* Water adds across a triple bond in the presence of dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and mercury(II) sulphate. The enol first formed rearranges to the ketone. Propyne gives propanone; ethyne is the exception and gives ethanal.

*From acyl chlorides.* An acyl chloride reacts with a dialkylcadmium to give a ketone.

*From nitriles.* A Grignard reagent adds to a nitrile, and hydrolysis of the intermediate imine gives a ketone.

*By Friedel-Crafts acylation.* Benzene reacts with an acyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ to give an aromatic ketone such as acetophenone.
Hydration of propyne gives propanone (ketone).
Friedel-Crafts acylation gives acetophenone.

blocks.problem: Identify A, B and C: benzene $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3COCl,\ anhyd.\ AlCl_3}}$ A $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn{-}Hg,\ conc.\ HCl}}$ B; and toluene $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2,\ CS_2;\ H_3O^+}}$ C. Name the reactions.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: Benzene and ethanoyl chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation. The acetyl group enters the ring, so A is acetophenone, $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$.

Step 2: Zinc amalgam with concentrated HCl is the Clemmensen reduction, which converts the C=O group to CH2. So B is ethylbenzene, $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3}$.

Step 3: Chromyl chloride in carbon disulphide followed by hydrolysis is the Etard reaction. It oxidises the methyl group of toluene only as far as the aldehyde, so C is benzaldehyde, $\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}$.
blocks.answer: A = acetophenone (Friedel-Crafts acylation); B = ethylbenzene (Clemmensen reduction); C = benzaldehyde (Etard reaction).

blocks.text: Physical properties of aldehydes and ketones: boiling point and solubility

**Boiling points.** Methanal is a gas and ethanal boils near room temperature; most other aldehydes and ketones are liquids. Because the carbonyl group is polar, molecules attract one another through dipole-dipole forces. These are stronger than the forces in non-polar hydrocarbons and ethers, so aldehydes and ketones boil higher than hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable molar mass. They cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, since there is no $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ or $\mathrm{N{-}H}$ bond, so they boil lower than alcohols and carboxylic acids of comparable mass.

blocks.caption: Boiling points of compounds of similar mass (approximate)

blocks.text:
The general order is: carboxylic acid > alcohol > aldehyde or ketone > ether > alkane (for similar mass).

**Solubility.** The oxygen of the carbonyl group can accept hydrogen bonds from water, so the lower members, methanal, ethanal and propanone, are miscible with water. As the length of the hydrocarbon part increases, the non-polar chain interferes with water's hydrogen bonding and solubility falls. Higher aldehydes and ketones are practically insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents. Methanal, ethanal and the other lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent smells, but higher aldehydes and many ketones have pleasant smells and are used in perfumes and flavourings.

**Common mistake.** Aldehydes and ketones can *accept* hydrogen bonds from water but cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves. That is why they dissolve in water but have lower boiling points than alcohols.
Chemical properties of aldehydes and ketones

The chemistry of aldehydes and ketones divides into nucleophilic addition, reduction, oxidation, reactions involving $\alpha$-hydrogen (aldol condensation) and a few special reactions of aldehydes (Cannizzaro) and of aromatic aldehydes.

**1. Nucleophilic addition and addition-elimination.**

*Hydrogen cyanide* adds to give a **cyanohydrin**. A trace of base generates the active nucleophile $\mathrm{CN^-}$. *Sodium hydrogensulphite* adds to give a crystalline bisulphite compound, which can be used to separate carbonyl compounds from other substances; the carbonyl compound can be regenerated by treating with dilute acid or base. *Alcohols* add in the presence of dry HCl. An aldehyde with one equivalent of alcohol gives a hemiacetal and with excess alcohol an acetal; a ketone with ethylene glycol gives a cyclic ketal. Acetals and ketals are stable to bases and can be hydrolysed back by dilute acid, so this is used to protect the carbonyl group.
Cyanohydrin formation (the product is a hydroxynitrile).

*Ammonia derivatives* ($\mathrm{H_2N{-}Z}$) add and then lose water, giving compounds with a $\mathrm{C{=}N{-}Z}$ group. Hydroxylamine gives an **oxime**, hydrazine gives a **hydrazone**, phenylhydrazine gives a phenylhydrazone, semicarbazide gives a **semicarbazone**, and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) gives a yellow, orange or red precipitate, the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. The 2,4-DNP test is a general test for aldehydes and ketones.
Condensation with ammonia derivatives; $\mathrm{Z = OH, NH_2, C_6H_5NH, NHCONH_2}$.

**2. Reduction.**

- To alcohols: $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$, $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ or $\mathrm{H_2/Ni}$ reduces aldehydes to primary and ketones to secondary alcohols.
- To hydrocarbons: **Clemmensen reduction** uses zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl (acidic conditions). **Wolff-Kishner reduction** converts the carbonyl group into a hydrazone with hydrazine and then heats it with potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol (basic conditions), releasing nitrogen. Both reactions replace $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ by $\mathrm{CH_2}$. Choose Clemmensen for substrates that survive acid and Wolff-Kishner for those that survive base.
Clemmensen reduction.
Wolff-Kishner reduction.

**3. Oxidation.** Aldehydes are easily oxidised even by mild oxidants, because the $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ bond of the $-\mathrm{CHO}$ group can be attacked. Ketones resist oxidation and are cleaved only by strong oxidants with the breaking of carbon-carbon bonds. This difference is used to tell aldehydes from ketones.

- **Tollens' test:** the reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate, $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}$. Aldehydes reduce it to metallic silver, which forms a bright **silver mirror** on the inside of the tube. Aromatic aldehydes also respond.
- **Fehling's test:** the reagent is an alkaline solution of copper(II) tartrate complex (blue). Aliphatic aldehydes reduce it to a **red-brown precipitate of cuprous oxide**, $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$. Aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde) do not respond, and ketones do not either.
- **Haloform (iodoform) reaction:** aldehydes and ketones with a $\mathrm{CH_3CO{-}}$ group (methyl ketones), and alcohols with a $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH){-}}$ group, react with sodium hypoiodite (iodine and NaOH) to give **yellow iodoform**, $\mathrm{CHI_3}$, and the sodium salt of the acid with one carbon less. Ethanal and propanone give the test; methanal and propanal do not.
Tollens' test: silver mirror.
Iodoform reaction of a methyl ketone.

**4. Aldol condensation (reaction of $\alpha$-hydrogen).** The hydrogens on the carbon next to the carbonyl group ($\alpha$-hydrogens) are acidic because the conjugate base (an enolate) is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl group. Aldehydes and ketones that have at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen, in the presence of dilute alkali, add to each other. Two molecules of ethanal give **3-hydroxybutanal** (aldol), a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde. On heating it loses water readily to give the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde but-2-enal. Ketones behave in the same way: propanone gives 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one, and that on heating loses water to give 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one.
Aldol addition followed by dehydration (aldol condensation).

**5. Cannizzaro reaction.** Aldehydes with **no $\alpha$-hydrogen** (methanal, benzaldehyde, 2,2-dimethylpropanal) undergo disproportionation when heated with concentrated alkali: one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate salt and the other is reduced to the alcohol.
Cannizzaro reaction of methanal.
Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde.

**6. Electrophilic substitution in aromatic carbonyl compounds.** In benzaldehyde and acetophenone the carbonyl group withdraws electrons from the ring and deactivates it. It is **meta-directing**. Nitration of benzaldehyde with $\mathrm{HNO_3/H_2SO_4}$ gives 3-nitrobenzaldehyde.

blocks.problem: Give one chemical test to distinguish between each pair: (a) pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one; (b) ethanal and propanal; (c) benzaldehyde and acetophenone; (d) ethanal and propanone.
blocks.solution:
(a) Pentan-2-one has a $\mathrm{CH_3CO{-}}$ group and gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform with $\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}$. Pentan-3-one has no methyl ketone group and gives no iodoform.

(b) Ethanal is $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ and has the $\mathrm{CH_3CO{-}}$ group, so it gives the iodoform test. Propanal does not.

(c) Acetophenone is a methyl ketone and gives iodoform, while benzaldehyde does not. Tollens' reagent can also be used, since benzaldehyde forms a silver mirror but acetophenone does not.

(d) Both give iodoform, since propanone is a methyl ketone. Tollens' test separates them: ethanal gives a silver mirror and propanone does not. Fehling's test also works.
blocks.answer: (a) iodoform: pentan-2-one positive; (b) iodoform: ethanal positive; (c) iodoform (or Tollens'): acetophenone positive (benzaldehyde gives Tollens'); (d) Tollens' or Fehling's: ethanal positive.

blocks.problem: Predict the products: (a) cross aldol-type self-condensation of propanone with dilute alkali, then heating; (b) benzaldehyde with concentrated NaOH; (c) 6.0 g of methanal under Cannizzaro conditions (molar masses: methanal 30 g/mol, methanol 32 g/mol); find the mass of methanol formed at 100% yield.
blocks.solution:
(a) Propanone has $\alpha$-hydrogens. Two molecules add to give 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one, and on heating it loses water to form 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one.

(b) Benzaldehyde has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, so the Cannizzaro reaction occurs. One molecule is oxidised to sodium benzoate and the other reduced to benzyl alcohol.

(c) Moles of methanal $= 6.0/30 = 0.20$ mol. The equation shows that 2 mol methanal gives 1 mol methanol and 1 mol sodium methanoate, so methanol formed $= 0.20/2 = 0.10$ mol. Mass of methanol $= 0.10 \times 32 = 3.2$ g.
blocks.answer: (a) 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (via the ketol); (b) benzyl alcohol + sodium benzoate; (c) 3.2 g of methanol.

blocks.text: **Exam tip.** Always check for $\alpha$-hydrogens. If the aldehyde has them, expect aldol condensation with *dilute* alkali. If it has none, expect Cannizzaro with *concentrated* alkali. Methanal has no $\alpha$-hydrogen (no carbon beside it), so it undergoes Cannizzaro.
Uses of aldehydes and ketones

**Methanal (formaldehyde).** A 40% aqueous solution, called **formalin**, is used to preserve biological specimens. Methanal condenses with phenol to give the thermosetting plastic **bakelite**, and with urea to make urea-formaldehyde resins.

**Ethanal (acetaldehyde).** It is used mainly as a starting material for ethanoic acid, ethyl ethanoate, vinyl acetate and other chemicals, and in making polymers and drugs.

**Propanone (acetone) and other ketones.** They are good solvents for paints, varnishes, lacquers and nail polish remover, and are starting materials in the synthesis of many compounds.

**Benzaldehyde.** It is used in perfumery and in the dye industry. Many aldehydes and ketones with pleasant odours are used in perfumes and flavourings, and many are used as solvents, as intermediates for drugs and polymers, and as reagents in the laboratory.

blocks.text: Formalin is a 40% aqueous solution of methanal. Methanal with phenol forms bakelite. Propanone is the commonest ketone solvent.
Structure of the carboxyl group

In a carboxylic acid the carboxyl carbon is $sp^2$ hybridised and bonded to the carbonyl oxygen (by a sigma and a $\pi$ bond), to the hydroxyl oxygen and to the R group. The group is **planar**, and the bond angles around the carbon are close to $120^\circ$. The oxygen of the $-\mathrm{OH}$ has a lone pair that is delocalised towards the carbonyl group by resonance. This has three important consequences.

1. The $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ bond is more polar and more easily broken, so the acid is far more acidic than an alcohol.
2. The carbonyl carbon is less positive than in an aldehyde or ketone. So carboxylic acids do not give the usual nucleophilic addition reactions of aldehydes and ketones (no 2,4-DNP precipitate, no Tollens' test).
3. When the proton is lost, the **carboxylate ion** has two equivalent $\mathrm{C{-}O}$ bonds, because the negative charge is shared equally between the two oxygens. This stabilises the anion and explains why carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than phenols or alcohols.
The two equivalent resonance forms of the carboxylate ion; the real ion has two identical $\mathrm{C{-}O}$ bonds.

Carboxylic acids are planar at the carboxyl carbon, and their anions are stabilised by resonance that spreads the charge over two oxygens. In the vapour phase and in non-polar solvents the molecules exist as **hydrogen-bonded cyclic dimers**.
Methods of preparation of carboxylic acids

**From primary alcohols and aldehydes.** Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by strong oxidising agents, such as acidified or alkaline potassium permanganate, acidified potassium dichromate or chromic acid. Aldehydes are oxidised to acids by the same reagents, and even by mild reagents such as Tollens' reagent.

**From alkylbenzenes.** Vigorous oxidation of an alkyl side chain of benzene with acidic or alkaline potassium permanganate (or chromic acid) converts the whole side chain, whatever its length, into a $-\mathrm{COOH}$ group, as long as there is a hydrogen on the carbon attached to the ring. Toluene, ethylbenzene and propylbenzene all give benzoic acid. A tertiary butyl group, which has no such hydrogen, is not oxidised.

**From nitriles and amides.** Hydrolysis of a nitrile with dilute acid or alkali gives first an amide and then a carboxylic acid (or its salt). Hydrolysis of an amide gives the acid in the same way.

**From Grignard reagents.** A Grignard reagent adds to solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) to give a carboxylate salt, which on acidification gives a carboxylic acid with one carbon more than the Grignard reagent.

**From acid derivatives.** Acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters are hydrolysed to carboxylic acids by water, acid or base.
Benzoic acid from toluene.
Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent; the chain is lengthened by one carbon.
Hydrolysis of a nitrile via the amide.

blocks.problem: Convert (a) bromoethane to propanoic acid by two different routes and (b) toluene to benzoic acid.
blocks.solution:
(a) Route 1 (Grignard): bromoethane with magnesium in dry ether gives ethylmagnesium bromide. Adding solid $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and then dilute acid gives propanoic acid, one carbon longer than the halide.

Route 2 (nitrile): bromoethane with alcoholic KCN gives propanenitrile, $\mathrm{C_2H_5CN}$, which on hydrolysis with dilute acid or alkali gives propanoic acid.

(b) The methyl group of toluene is oxidised by hot alkaline potassium permanganate to a carboxylate, and acidification gives benzoic acid.
blocks.answer: (a) $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br \to C_2H_5MgBr \to C_2H_5COOH}$ (with $\mathrm{CO_2}$) or $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br \to C_2H_5CN \to C_2H_5COOH}$; (b) $\mathrm{KMnO_4/KOH}$, heat, then $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$.

blocks.text: **Exam tip.** The Grignard route and the nitrile route both lengthen the carbon chain: the Grignard adds one carbon through $\mathrm{CO_2}$, and the nitrile route adds one carbon through $\mathrm{CN^-}$. Oxidation routes keep the carbon number the same.
Physical properties of carboxylic acids: boiling point and solubility

**Boiling points.** Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of comparable molar mass. The reason is extensive hydrogen bonding: two carboxylic acid molecules join through two hydrogen bonds to form a stable **cyclic dimer**, which makes each unit effectively twice as large and takes much energy to separate. Ethanoic acid boils at 391 K, higher than propan-1-ol (370 K) of nearly the same mass. Methanoic acid boils at about 374 K and propanoic acid at about 414 K.

**Solubility.** Carboxylic acids with up to about four carbon atoms are miscible with water because they hydrogen bond with water through both the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl group. Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens. Benzoic acid, with a large non-polar ring, is nearly insoluble in cold water but dissolves in hot water. All carboxylic acids dissolve in less polar solvents such as ether, alcohol and benzene.

The first three acids are pungent liquids (ethanoic acid smells of vinegar), the middle members (up to nine carbons) are oily liquids with an unpleasant smell, and the higher acids are odourless waxy solids.
Dimerisation of carboxylic acids through hydrogen bonding.

**Common mistake.** The molar mass of a carboxylic acid measured by freezing point or boiling point in benzene appears to be double its real value, because the acid exists as a dimer in non-polar solvents.
Chemical properties of carboxylic acids

**Acidity.** Carboxylic acids are weak acids. They ionise in water to give the carboxylate ion and the hydronium ion, but they are far stronger than alcohols and phenols. Typical pKa values: methanoic acid 3.75, benzoic acid 4.19, ethanoic acid 4.76, phenol about 10, ethanol about 16. The acid dissociation constant is $K_a = 10^{-pK_a}$, so ethanoic acid has $K_a = 10^{-4.76} = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}$.

*Effect of substituents.* Electron-withdrawing groups (halogens, $-\mathrm{NO_2}$) near the carboxyl group stabilise the carboxylate by their $-I$ effect and increase acidity. Their effect grows with the number of such groups and falls rapidly with distance. Electron-releasing groups ($-\mathrm{CH_3}$ and other alkyl groups) destabilise the carboxylate and decrease acidity. So $\mathrm{FCH_2COOH}$ (pKa 2.66) is stronger than $\mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}$ (2.86), which is stronger than $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ (4.76). Methanoic acid, with no alkyl group, is stronger than ethanoic acid. Benzoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid because the $sp^2$ carbon of the phenyl group is electron-withdrawing relative to an alkyl carbon.
A smaller $pK_a$ means a larger $K_a$ and a stronger acid.

**Reactions of the O-H group.** Carboxylic acids react with active metals to release hydrogen, and with alkalis and with sodium carbonate and **sodium hydrogencarbonate** to give salts, water (or $\mathrm{H_2O + CO_2}$). The brisk effervescence of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ with $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ is a simple test that separates carboxylic acids from phenols, which do not react with bicarbonate.

**Esterification.** An acid heated with an alcohol and a little concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ gives an ester in a reversible reaction (Fischer esterification). The reaction is driven forward by removing water or using excess of one reactant.

**Formation of acid derivatives.** $\mathrm{SOCl_2}$ (best, because $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ escape as gases), $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ or $\mathrm{PCl_3}$ convert $\mathrm{R{-}COOH}$ to the acid chloride $\mathrm{RCOCl}$. Heating with a strong dehydrating agent such as $\mathrm{P_2O_5}$ gives the acid anhydride. Reaction with ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which on heating loses water to form the **amide**.
Esterification.
Acid chloride formation.
Amide formation.

**Reduction.** Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols by $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ or by diborane, $\mathrm{B_2H_6}$. Sodium borohydride does not reduce them.

**Decarboxylation.** The sodium salt of a carboxylic acid, heated with soda lime ($\mathrm{NaOH + CaO}$), loses $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and gives an alkane with one carbon fewer. Electrolysis of the aqueous sodium salt (Kolbe electrolysis) gives the alkane $\mathrm{R{-}R}$ at the anode.

**Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction.** A carboxylic acid with an $\alpha$-hydrogen is treated with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a little red phosphorus, and then with water. The $\alpha$-hydrogen is replaced by halogen, giving an $\alpha$-halo acid.

**Ring substitution in benzoic acid.** The $-\mathrm{COOH}$ group deactivates the ring and is meta-directing. Nitration gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid. Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions, because the ring is strongly deactivated and the carboxyl group complexes with $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$.
Decarboxylation with soda lime: $\mathrm{CH_3COONa \to CH_4}$.
HVZ reaction: $\alpha$-halogenation of a carboxylic acid.
Reduction of a carboxylic acid.

blocks.problem: Compare the acidities of ethanoic acid ($pK_a = 4.76$) and chloroethanoic acid ($pK_a = 2.86$): calculate $K_a$(chloroethanoic) / $K_a$(ethanoic) and explain the result. Then arrange in increasing acid strength: ethanoic acid, methanoic acid, benzoic acid, chloroethanoic acid, phenol.
blocks.solution:
Since $K_a = 10^{-pK_a}$, the ratio is $10^{-2.86}/10^{-4.76} = 10^{(4.76-2.86)} = 10^{1.90} \approx 79$. So chloroethanoic acid is about 79 times stronger.

Explanation: chlorine withdraws electrons through the sigma bonds (the $-I$ effect). It spreads the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it, so the acid ionises more readily. The methyl group of ethanoic acid does the opposite.

Order of strength using pKa: phenol (about 10) < ethanoic acid (4.76) < benzoic acid (4.19) < methanoic acid (3.75) < chloroethanoic acid (2.86). Remember that a lower pKa means a stronger acid.
blocks.answer: Ratio about 79; increasing acidity: phenol < ethanoic acid < benzoic acid < methanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid.

blocks.problem: Distinguish between (a) methanoic acid and ethanoic acid; (b) benzoic acid and phenol; (c) ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate. Then find A and B: sodium ethanoate $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{soda\ lime,\ heat}}$ A; propanoic acid $\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2/red\ P,\ then\ H_2O}}$ B.
blocks.solution:
(a) Methanoic acid contains an aldehyde-like $\mathrm{H{-}C(=O)}$ unit and so reduces Tollens' reagent to a silver mirror (and decolourises acidified permanganate), but ethanoic acid does not.

(b) Benzoic acid is stronger than carbonic acid and liberates $\mathrm{CO_2}$ with aqueous $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$. Phenol does not. Phenol also gives a violet colour with neutral $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$.

(c) Ethanoic acid gives effervescence with $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$, but the ester does not.

A: Decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate with soda lime removes one carbon as sodium carbonate and gives methane, $\mathrm{CH_4}$.

B: HVZ reaction brominates the carbon next to the carboxyl group. B is 2-bromopropanoic acid, $\mathrm{CH_3CHBrCOOH}$.
blocks.answer: (a) Tollens' test; (b) $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ (or $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$) test; (c) $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ test; A = methane; B = 2-bromopropanoic acid.

blocks.text: **Common mistake.** In the HVZ reaction the halogen enters the $\alpha$-position, not the carboxyl carbon, and the acid must have at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen. Methanoic acid and benzoic acid cannot undergo it.
Uses of carboxylic acids

**Methanoic acid** is used in the rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating industries. **Ethanoic acid** is used as a solvent and as a starting material for esters, cellulose acetate fibres (rayon) and many other chemicals; vinegar is a dilute solution (about 5-8%) of ethanoic acid and is used as a food preservative and flavouring. **Hexanedioic acid** (adipic acid) is the starting material for the synthetic polymer nylon-6,6. **Esters of benzoic acid** are used in perfumery, and sodium benzoate is a food preservative. **Higher fatty acids** are used to make soaps and detergents, and some are used in the manufacture of polishes, candles and lubricants.
Vinegar is dilute ethanoic acid. Hexanedioic acid gives nylon-6,6. Sodium benzoate is a food preservative. Higher fatty acids give soaps.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}$ is
questions.explanation: The compound has four carbons with a carbonyl group inside the chain, so it is a ketone, named with the suffix -one. Numbering from the end that gives the carbonyl carbon the lower number puts it at C-2, giving butan-2-one (ethyl methyl ketone).

optionRationale.1: Butanal is an aldehyde with the -CHO at the end of the chain.
optionRationale.3: Pentan-2-one has five carbons, one more than the given structure.
optionRationale.4: Butan-2-ol is an alcohol, but the given compound has no -OH group.

questions.objective: Name ketones by IUPAC rules

questions.stem: Benzoyl chloride is converted to benzaldehyde by
options: $\mathrm{H_2}$ over palladium on barium sulphate (Rosenmund reduction)
questions.explanation: The Rosenmund reduction hydrogenates an acyl chloride over palladium supported on barium sulphate. The catalyst is partially poisoned so that the reduction stops at the aldehyde stage and does not go on to the alcohol. Hydride reagents are strong enough to reduce the acyl chloride to the alcohol.

optionRationale.1: LiAlH4 is a strong reductant and takes the acyl chloride to the primary alcohol.
optionRationale.2: NaBH4 reduces the acyl chloride beyond the aldehyde to the alcohol.
optionRationale.4: Clemmensen conditions reduce a C=O group to CH2 and are not used on acyl chlorides.

questions.objective: Recall the Rosenmund reduction

questions.stem: Which of the following gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes to carboxylate ions and is itself reduced to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror. Ethanal is an aldehyde, whereas the other three compounds are ketones, which are not oxidised by Tollens' reagent.

optionRationale.1: Propanone is a ketone and does not reduce Tollens' reagent.
optionRationale.2: Benzophenone is a ketone and gives no silver mirror.
optionRationale.3: Butan-2-one is a ketone and gives no reaction with Tollens' reagent.

questions.objective: Use Tollens' test to identify aldehydes

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: The four compounds have similar molar masses (about 58-60). Ethanoic acid forms a stable cyclic dimer with two hydrogen bonds, giving it the highest boiling point (391 K). Propan-1-ol forms hydrogen bonds (370 K), propanal has only dipole forces (322 K) and methoxyethane is the least polar (281 K).

optionRationale.2: Propan-1-ol has H-bonding, but it forms no dimer and so boils lower than the acid.
optionRationale.4: Methoxyethane has no O-H bond and boils lowest.

questions.objective: Compare boiling points across oxygen-containing families

questions.stem: The $pK_a$ of ethanoic acid is 4.76 and that of chloroethanoic acid is 2.86. The ratio $K_a(\mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}) / K_a(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})$ is approximately
questions.explanation: Since Ka = 10^(-pKa), the ratio equals 10^(4.76 - 2.86) = 10^1.90, which is about 79. The result shows that chloroethanoic acid is nearly eighty times stronger than ethanoic acid because the electron-withdrawing chlorine stabilises the carboxylate ion.

optionRationale.1: 1.9 is the difference of pKa values, not the ratio of Ka values.
optionRationale.2: 7.9 comes from taking 10^0.9, which wrongly uses a pKa difference of 0.9.
optionRationale.4: 190 is just 100 times the pKa difference and has no basis in the calculation.

questions.objective: Calculate relative acid strengths from pKa

questions.stem: Which of the following undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated NaOH?
questions.explanation: The Cannizzaro reaction needs an aldehyde that has no alpha-hydrogen. 2,2-Dimethylpropanal has a quaternary carbon next to the CHO group, so it has none, and it disproportionates into the alcohol and carboxylate. Ethanal and propanal have alpha-hydrogens and undergo aldol reaction, and butan-2-one is a ketone.

optionRationale.1: Ethanal has alpha-hydrogens and gives aldol condensation instead.
optionRationale.3: Propanal has alpha-hydrogens and is aldol-active.
optionRationale.4: Butan-2-one is a ketone, and the Cannizzaro reaction is for aldehydes.

questions.objective: Identify substrates for the Cannizzaro reaction

questions.stem: Ethanal on treatment with dilute NaOH and then heating gives
questions.explanation: Two ethanal molecules undergo aldol addition to give 3-hydroxybutanal. On heating, this beta-hydroxy aldehyde loses a molecule of water and forms the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde but-2-enal. This overall process is the aldol condensation.

optionRationale.2: 3-Hydroxybutanal is the intermediate aldol product before dehydration.
optionRationale.3: Butanal would need reduction of the aldol, which does not occur here.
optionRationale.4: The hydroxyl group is formed at carbon 3, not carbon 2.

questions.objective: Predict the aldol condensation product

questions.stem: Propanoic acid is treated with $\mathrm{Br_2}$ and a little red phosphorus, and then with water. The product is
options: propanoyl bromide as the final isolated product
questions.explanation: This is the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction. Halogen with red phosphorus replaces a hydrogen on the alpha carbon, the carbon next to the carboxyl group. Subsequent hydrolysis with water restores the acid group and gives 2-bromopropanoic acid.

optionRationale.1: Halogenation occurs at the alpha carbon, which is C-2, not at C-3.
optionRationale.2: Bromoethane would be formed by decarboxylation, which does not occur here.
optionRationale.3: The acyl bromide intermediate is hydrolysed by the water in the second step.

questions.objective: Apply the HVZ reaction

questions.stem: 6.0 g of methanal (molar mass 30 g/mol) is treated with concentrated NaOH. Assuming complete conversion, the mass of methanol (32 g/mol) formed is
questions.explanation: Moles of methanal are 6.0/30 = 0.20 mol. In the Cannizzaro reaction 2 mol of methanal give 1 mol of methanol and 1 mol of sodium methanoate, so 0.10 mol of methanol is formed. Its mass is 0.10 x 32 = 3.2 g.

optionRationale.1: 1.6 g would correspond to 0.05 mol, a quarter of the methanal.
optionRationale.2: 2.0 g does not correspond to any simple ratio of the moles here.
optionRationale.4: 6.4 g wrongly assumes one mole of methanol per mole of methanal.

questions.objective: Do stoichiometry for the Cannizzaro reaction

questions.stem: A ketone with an acid-sensitive group must be converted to the corresponding $\mathrm{CH_2}$ compound. Which reagent should be used?
options: $\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}$, then KOH in ethylene glycol on heating
questions.explanation: Replacing C=O by CH2 is done by the Clemmensen reduction (acidic) or the Wolff-Kishner reduction (basic). When the substrate is acid-sensitive, Wolff-Kishner is chosen because it is carried out in base. NaBH4 and LiAlH4 only give the alcohol.

optionRationale.1: Clemmensen reduction uses concentrated HCl, which an acid-sensitive group would not survive.
optionRationale.3: NaBH4 only reduces the ketone to an alcohol.
optionRationale.4: LiAlH4 also gives the alcohol, not the hydrocarbon.

questions.objective: Choose between Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reduction

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
Reason (R): The carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde carries a greater partial positive charge and is less sterically hindered.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: An aldehyde has one alkyl group and one hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, whereas a ketone has two alkyl groups. The alkyl groups release electrons and reduce the positive charge, and they also hinder the approach of the nucleophile. So (R) correctly explains (A).

optionRationale.2: Both are true and the reason is the correct explanation.
optionRationale.3: (R) is the real cause of the greater reactivity, not just a side fact.
optionRationale.4: (R) is a true statement and explains (A).

questions.objective: Explain the reactivity order of carbonyl compounds

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Benzaldehyde does not reduce Fehling's solution.
Reason (R): Benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling's solution, so (A) is true. (R) is also true, since benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen, but this fact is not the reason. Fehling's solution is a mild oxidising agent, and benzaldehyde, whose carbonyl is conjugated with the ring, is not oxidised easily enough by it.

optionRationale.1: The absence of an alpha-hydrogen governs the Cannizzaro and aldol reactions, not oxidation by Fehling's solution.
optionRationale.3: (A) is correct, as aromatic aldehydes do not respond to Fehling's test.
optionRationale.4: (R) is a correct fact about benzaldehyde.

questions.objective: Distinguish aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes in Fehling's test

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Carboxylic acids liberate carbon dioxide from sodium hydrogencarbonate.
Reason (R): Carboxylic acids are weaker acids than carbonic acid.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4-5) are stronger than carbonic acid (pKa about 6.4), so they displace carbon dioxide from bicarbonate with effervescence and (A) is true. (R) states the reverse of the actual order of acid strengths, so it is false.

optionRationale.1: (R) is false, so the pair cannot be both true.
optionRationale.2: (A) is true, so this option wrongly rejects it.
optionRationale.4: (A) is true; the option claiming it false is wrong.

questions.objective: Use the bicarbonate test for carboxylic acids

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Methanal gives a positive iodoform test.
Reason (R): The iodoform test is given by compounds containing the $\mathrm{CH_3CO{-}}$ or $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH){-}}$ group.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Methanal has neither a CH3CO- group nor a CH3CH(OH)- group, so it does not give the iodoform test, and (A) is false. (R) correctly states the structural requirement for the test (as in ethanal, propanone and ethanol), so (R) is true.

optionRationale.1: (A) is false, since methanal lacks the required group.
optionRationale.2: (A) is false, so neither 'both true' option applies.
optionRationale.3: (R) is true, so this option is wrong to call it false.

questions.objective: State the structural requirement for the iodoform test

questions.stem: Match the named reaction in List-I with the reagent or feature in List-II.

right: IV. SnCl2/HCl, then H3O+ (on a nitrile)

questions.explanation: The Rosenmund reduction uses H2 with Pd-BaSO4 (II). The Etard reaction uses CrO2Cl2 in CS2 (I). The Stephen reaction uses SnCl2/HCl followed by hydrolysis of a nitrile (IV). The Gattermann-Koch reaction uses CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl3 and CuCl (III).

optionRationale.1: Rosenmund and Etard are interchanged in this code.
optionRationale.2: Stephen and Gattermann-Koch are interchanged in this code.
optionRationale.4: Rosenmund and Stephen are wrongly paired.

questions.objective: Match named reactions with reagents

questions.stem: Match the test in List-I with the observation in List-II.
questions.explanation: Ethanal gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent (II) and a red-brown precipitate of Cu2O with Fehling's solution (IV). Propanone gives an orange or yellow precipitate with 2,4-DNP (I) and a yellow precipitate of iodoform with NaOI (III).

optionRationale.2: Tollens' and Fehling's observations are interchanged here.
optionRationale.3: The 2,4-DNP and iodoform observations are interchanged here.
optionRationale.4: Tollens' test is wrongly assigned the 2,4-DNP precipitate.

questions.objective: Match tests with their observations

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about carboxylic acids.
A. Methanoic acid reduces Tollens' reagent.
B. Nitration of benzoic acid gives mainly the meta product.
C. Sodium borohydride reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.
D. Heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime gives methane.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Methanoic acid has an aldehyde-like H-C(=O) unit and reduces Tollens' reagent. The carboxyl group is meta-directing, so nitration of benzoic acid gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid. Soda lime decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate gives methane. Statement C is false since NaBH4 cannot reduce carboxylic acids.

optionRationale.1: C is false, so any option containing it is wrong.
optionRationale.2: C is false and A is true, so this option fails.
optionRationale.3: C is false, so the option containing it is wrong.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on reactions of carboxylic acids

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about aldehydes and ketones.
A. The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised and the group is planar.
B. The carbonyl carbon bears a partial positive charge.
C. Aldehydes and ketones form hydrogen bonds with each other.
D. Lower aldehydes and ketones are miscible with water.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is sp2 and trigonal planar, and it carries a partial positive charge because oxygen is more electronegative. Lower members such as ethanal and propanone are miscible with water through hydrogen bonds with water. Statement C is false because they lack an O-H bond and cannot hydrogen bond with each other.

optionRationale.1: C is false, so options with C are wrong.
optionRationale.3: Statements A and B are true, and D is also true, so this option is the complete set.
optionRationale.4: C is false and A is true, so this option fails.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on structure and properties of carbonyl compounds

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Aldol condensation requires at least one alpha-hydrogen.
B. Benzaldehyde undergoes aldol condensation in dilute NaOH.
C. Methanal with concentrated NaOH gives methanol and sodium methanoate.
D. The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Aldol condensation needs an alpha-hydrogen to form the enolate. The Cannizzaro reaction of methanal gives methanol and sodium methanoate, and it is a disproportionation because one molecule is oxidised and another reduced. Statement B is false, since benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen.

optionRationale.2: B is false, so this option containing it is wrong.
optionRationale.3: B is false, so this option is wrong.
optionRationale.4: B is false, and A is true, so this option fails.

questions.objective: Compare aldol and Cannizzaro reactions

questions.stem: Benzene is treated with $\mathrm{CH_3COCl}$ and anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ to give X. X is heated with $\mathrm{I_2}$ and NaOH, and the mixture is acidified. The organic acid obtained is
questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts acylation gives acetophenone, a methyl ketone. Iodine and NaOH bring about the iodoform reaction: the methyl group is converted to CHI3 and the rest of the molecule becomes sodium benzoate. Acidification then gives benzoic acid, which has one carbon fewer than acetophenone.

optionRationale.1: Phenylacetic acid has the same carbon count as the ketone and does not form in the iodoform reaction.
optionRationale.2: Ethanoic acid would mean the phenyl group is lost, which does not happen.
optionRationale.3: Benzaldehyde is not the product of the iodoform reaction; an acid is formed.

questions.objective: Predict the product of a multi-step carbonyl sequence
